    DUE TO TARIFF VIOLATIONS THROUGH THE DESIGNATION OF SHORT-TERM
            RELIABILITY PROJECTS IN THE 2025 TRANSMISSION PLAN

           Pursuant to Sections 206, 306, and 309 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) 1 and Rule 206

of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or

the “Commission”),2 the Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition (“ETCC”) and the

Industrial Energy Consumers of America (“IECA”) (collectively, “Complainants”) submit this

Complaint against Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”) and the SPP Board of Directors (“Board”)

for violating Attachment Y, Section I.3 of the SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT” or

“Tariff”).3 Complainants herein demonstrate that the SPP Board violated SPP’s Tariff on February

3, 2026 by designating four projects (“Four Projects”),4 expected to cost $3.8 billion and not

 projected to be available until 2029-2030, as Short-Term Reliability Projects under the 2025

Integrated Transmission Planning (“ITP”) portfolio. The evidence in this Complaint and

supporting affidavits5 demonstrates that SPP’s designation of the exemption for immediate need

reliability projects is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential because SPP

does not adequately show the Four Projects, including two which will provide service at 765

kilovolts (“kV”), are “required to be in service within three years or less to address an identified

reliability violation.”6 SPP failed to explain “[t]he circumstances that generated the immediate

reliability need” and failed to provide “an explanation of why that immediate reliability need was

not identified earlier.”7 SPP failed to provide explanations of non-transmission solutions

considered.8 And SPP and its Board have not supported the Short-Term Reliability Project

determinations with transparency and sufficient documentation, “to allow stakeholders to

understand the need and why it is time sensitive.”9 Consistent with FERC’s statutory duty to

ensure just and reasonable rates and its mission to ensure energy affordability, the

Commission must act now to prevent consumers in SPP from paying millions of dollars in

excess charges for transmission in both in the near- and long-term.

           Section 206(a) of the Federal Power Act ensures “the protection of the public interest, as

distinguished from the private interests of the utilities.”10 Commission regulations implementing

Section 20611 provide that “[a]ny person may file a complaint seeking Commission action against

law administered by the Commission, or for any other alleged wrong over which the

Commission may have jurisdiction.”12 The Commission reviews tariff violations under section

206 of the FPA.13 Therefore, Complainants respectfully request that FERC: (1) find that SPP and

the Board violated the Tariff; (2) and direct SPP to comply with the Tariff, including through

necessary revisions to the 2025 ITP portfolio to ensure that SPP expeditiously initiates the

Transmission Owner Selection Process to competitively select Designated Transmission Owners

for the Four Projects. The Commission must direct SPP to reevaluate the Short-Term Reliability

Project designation of the Four Projects classified under the 2025 ITP portfolio and issue any and

all additional relief necessary to ensure that SPP complies with its Tariff on a going forward-basis

and only uses the Short-Term Reliability Project designation in “limited circumstances,” as

required by this Commission’s precedent and prior directives.14 Complainants respectfully request

expedited processing of this Complaint to ensure the timely development of necessary

transmission in a cost-effective manner.

I.         SUMMARY OF COMPLAINT

           SPP violated Attachment Y, Section I.3 of the SPP Tariff through SPP’s application of the

“short-term reliability” exemption (“Short-Term Reliability Project Exemption”) based on the

 filed public comments contending that the Board should not apply the Short-Term Reliability

Project designation to the Four Projects, the Board nonetheless applied the designation and

exempted the projects from mandated competition without adequately addressing stakeholder

concerns or justifying application of the designation and exemption. Notably, of the twenty-two

stakeholder comments submitted, sixteen advocated for transmission competition and a focus on

the “in-service” language of Attachment Y, as well as the overall lack of project cost and schedule

accountability outside the competitive process.20

           This Complaint is specific to SPP’s Tariff violations stemming from the Board’s approval

of the 2025 STRP Report and thus the inappropriate designation of the Four Projects as Short-

Term Reliability Projects. Historical evidence shows an evolving SPP pattern of abusing the Short-

Term Reliability Project designation and failing to provide support for its designations with

adequate transparency in its ITP process, despite SPP’s prior averment to the Commission (where

SPP initially proposed Attachment Y provisions) that it did not expect a need to invoke the Short-

and efficient regional planning.

             Witness Richard Allen, a transmission development consultant with nearly 40 years of

experience, assesses that four to seven years is a reasonable planning range for a greenfield 345

kV project36, while recent 765 kV projects he studied had projected in-service dates approximately

nine years after approval – in stark contrast to the 5-year in-service dates assigned by SPP for both

of its 765 kV Short-Term Reliability Projects (Crawfish Draw – Phantom and Seminole –

Southwest Shreveport).37 Therefore, “SPP’s projected in-service dates indicate that the permanent

transmission solutions will not address the identified reliability violations within the three-year

period,” as required by Attachment Y.38 Witness Allen makes the important distinction that, “A

reliability need date identifies when SPP states that a reliability violation must be addressed. That

date remains a relevant benchmark for determining whether a project is delivered when needed,

but it does not establish that the permanent transmission solution physically can be completed by

that date.”39 And to the proposition that subjecting the Four Projects to competitive solicitation

would cause delay, Witness Allen testifies:

                     I do not believe the available information supports the conclusion
                     that directly assigned projects generally proceed faster than
                     competitively awarded projects. A directly assigned project may be
                     developed and completed faster than a competitively awarded
                     project in a particular case, but that does not establish that directly
                     assigned projects, as a class, proceed more quickly. Project
                     schedules depend on the project’s scope and complexity, siting and
                     permitting requirements, land acquisition needs, the developer’s
                     execution plan and available resources, equipment and material lead
                     times, construction conditions, and other project specific factors.40

 Complainants’ three witnesses demonstrate that 1) the Four Projects cannot meet the requirement

that to be a Short-Term Reliability Project the facility is required to be placed in service in three

years or less; 2) the explanation required by the Tariff for each Short-Term Reliability Project

designation was not provided to stakeholders by SPP in accordance with Tariff Attachment Y; 3)

the 765 kV projects cannot feasibly be placed in-service within three years; 4) evidence does not

demonstrate that competition delays project in-service dates; and 5) competition does offer

consumers protection against unbridled project costs.

       Tariff-based obligations of RTOs like SPP, borne out of Commission orders and legislation,

mandate SPP to act reasonably and without undue discrimination in its functions, including

transmission planning. Order No. 100041 enshrined the competitive process into RTO transmission

planning. However, SPP has effectuated its ITP process without due consideration to either

consumers or non-incumbent competitive developers, abusing the Short-Term Reliability Project

exemption and definition of reliability “need” in contravention of the plain language in SPP’s Tariff

and to the advantage of incumbent utilities and SPP itself. Not only does SPP’s abuse of the Short-

Term Reliability Project designation to exempt Extra High Voltage (“EHV”) and Ultra High

Voltage (“UHV”) projects from the default requirement for competition violate the filed rate, but

also exacerbate the energy affordability crisis in the long-term given the expected service life of

the projects. Accordingly, SPP’s actions are directly contrary to the Commission’s mission to

“[a]ssist consumers in obtaining reliable, safe, secure, and economically efficient energy services

at a reasonable cost through appropriate regulatory and market means, and collaborative

          In promulgating Order No. 1920, the Commission explained:

                    The electric transmission grid is the backbone of the American
                    economy and essential to the national security of our country. The
                    mission of this agency is to ensure reliable, safe, secure, and
                    economically efficient energy for consumers at a reasonable cost.
                    Ensuring we have a robust, well-planned electric transmission grid
                    is the single most important step that this Commission can take to
                    fulfill that statutory mandate.44

To meet its mission to protect consumers from escalating transmission rates – the fastest growing

part of consumer electricity bills45 – the Commission must ensure two things: (1) that the

appropriate transmission projects are planned; and (2) that those planned transmission projects are

implemented in an economically efficient manner, which requires strict adherence with the Tariff

language geared toward ensuring that economically efficient implementation.

           To meet its statutory obligations, the Commission can and should apply such principles to

SPP’s 2025 ITP assessment by (1) requiring SPP to align its application of the Short-Term

Reliability Project exemption with the plain language of the Tariff, and (2) requiring SPP to

establish that projects designated as Short-Term Reliability Projects are capable of meeting the

Tariff requirement to be in-service within 3 years or less to be excluded from competition. Absent

this Complaint, FERC will have no opportunity to consider the concerns raised by stakeholders

         The relief Complainants seek is a requirement that SPP apply the filed rate, the Tariff, as

written, thus expeditiously initiating the Transmission Owner Selection Process to competitively

select developers for the Four Projects which were improperly excluded from competition. Given

that SPP may effectuate a direct assignment of the Four Projects in early February 2027, as well

as potentially designating additional projects as Short-Term Reliability Projects, Complainants

respectfully ask the Commission to issue an order on this Complaint in advance of February 2027

and direct SPP to comply with its Tariff and Order No. 1000.

economic growth, quality of life for our citizens, and the competitiveness of American

industry. IECA promotes the interests of manufacturing companies through advocacy and

           A.       Order No. 1000 and its Subsequent Legal Challenges
           The Commission eliminated federal rights of first refusal (“ROFRs”) in Order No 1000,

mandating competitive solicitations processes for RTOs in most instances when regional cost

allocation was to be employed. The Commission held that any exemptions to those competitive

requirements, here Attachment Y, must be used narrowly in “limited circumstances.”50

             In Order No. 1000, the Commission held that it cannot effectively establish just and

reasonable transmission rates when rights of first refusal are present. Stated differently, incumbent

preferences prevent the Commission from meeting its statutory consumer protection mandate to

ensure just and reasonable transmission rates. In Order No. 1000, the Commission held that “the

elimination of federal rights of first refusal from Commission-jurisdictional tariffs and agreements

is necessary and appropriate to ensure that rates for jurisdictional services are just and

reasonable.”51 That finding remains as true today as it was when the Commission issued Order

No. 1000. In fact, given the need to strengthen the aging grid in an affordable manner, that finding

becomes even more important today.

            In Order No. 1000, the Commission found “there is a need to act at this time to remove

provisions from Commission-jurisdictional tariffs and agreements that grant incumbent

transmission providers a federal right of first refusal to construct transmission facilities selected in

a regional transmission plan for purposes of cost allocation.”52 The Commission further found that

federal rights of first refusal could “lead[] to rates for jurisdictional transmission service that are

unjust and unreasonable”53 because “it is not in the economic self-interest of incumbent

transmission providers to permit new entrants to develop transmission facilities, even if proposals

submitted by new entrants would result in a more efficient or cost-effective solution to the region’s

needs.”54 The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit (“D.C. Circuit”)

upheld the Commission’s pro-transmission competition findings in Order No. 1000, explaining

that “basic economic principles make clear that rights of first refusal are likely to have a direct

            B.      Development of SPP’s Tariff Attachment Y.
           Following issuance of Order No. 1000, SPP, like other RTOs, was required to submit a

compliance filing to the Commission outlining its proposed tariff revisions to satisfy the Order No.

1000 directives. In SPP’s first Order No. 1000 Compliance Filing,74 SPP proposed its short-term

reliability exemption. The Commission partially accepted SPP’s proposal, explaining that in cases

of projects needed to resolve a time-sensitive reliability criteria violation, it was just and reasonable

proposed reliability-based exception to ROFR removal, the Commission established five

generic criteria with the goal of placing reasonable bounds on an RTO’s discretion to determine

whether there is sufficient time to permit competition. The five criteria are as follows (“Immediate

Need Criteria”):

           supported written description explaining: (1) the decision to designate an
           incumbent transmission owner as the entity responsible for construction and
           ownership of the project, including an explanation of other transmission or non-
           transmission options that the region considered; and (2) the circumstances that

  VI.     OTHER REQUIRED INFORMATION FOR COMPLIANCE WITH RULE 206

        A.      Identification of the action or inaction (18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(1))

        As discussed fully in the Complaint, the action violating the Commission’s obligation to

ensure just and reasonable transmission rates is the application by the SPP Board of the Short-

Term Reliability Project exemption in violation of Attachment Y of the SPP Tariff.

        B.      Explanation of the Violation (18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(2))

        As fully recounted in the Complaint, the Commission has made clear that Short-Term

Reliability Project designations are meant to be applied in limited circumstances of immediate

reliability need. In SPP’s Tariff, that is defined as required to be in service in three years or less to

address the reliability violation. The current application of the Tariff by SPP and the SPP Board of

the Short-Term Reliability Project exemption violates the plain language of the Tariff. SPP’s use

of the short-term designation to exclude over $3.8 billion in transmission from competition is a

direct and clear violation of the Tariff and an afront to Commission directives borne out of Order

No. 1000 that incumbent preferences be removed. As outlined fully in the Complaint, the violation

is the failure of SPP and the SPP Board to apply the Tariff and thus to ensure just and reasonable

rates, as well as non-preferential practices in its designation of transmission projects as Short-Term

Reliability Projects exempt from the competitive process. Such practice threatens competitive

integrity in the transmission sector and directly affects the costs borne by ratepayers. The

Commission is obligated by sections 206 and 309 to address these Tariff violations and ensure they

result in just and reasonable rates.

           Complainants represent large end-use consumers, consumer advocates, public interest

organizations, nonincumbent developers, and thinktanks. As recognized by the Commission in

Order No. 1920, the transmission component of a consumer’s bill has been substantially increasing

in recent years. Order No. 1920 found that “transmission spending has continued to increase

nationwide.”287 The Commission recognized in Order No. 1920 that transmission costs have

become an increasing share of customers’ overall electricity bills, underscoring the importance of

ensuring that transmission investments are efficient and cost-effective.288 Transmission developers

invested approximately $20-$25 billion annually in transmission facilities in the United States

from 2013-2020.289 The Commission found that the “record demonstrates that transmission

investment is likely to substantially increase in coming years”290 and there will be “sustained

transmission spending through at least 2050.”291 In the absence of competitive solicitations,

consumers will continue to be subjected to paying unjust and unreasonable rates associated with

           Pertinent to the Commission’s statutory consumer protection mandate, when competition

has occurred, transmission developers (including incumbent developers forced to compete) have

offered consumer beneficial terms and conditions to transmission development and ownership that

are absent when projects are just handed to incumbent developers.292 As such, the experience since

Order No. 1000 demonstrates that competition helps ensure that transmission rates are just and

reasonable.293 Further, the Commission has found that the contractual agreements arising through

the Order No. 1000-mandated competitive processes themselves provide consumer benefits above

and beyond any obligation arising from transmission owner agreements.294 The Commission was

clear in Order No. 1000 that the need for a competitive test to ensure just and reasonable rates

crossed all transmission drivers, rejecting calls for an exclusion for reliability projects, 295 and

extending the competitive requirement to projects needed to meet public policy requirements.296

FERC’s national directive in Order No. 1000 to remove anti-competitive, self-granted, incumbent

preferences applies fully to an RTO’s transmission planning processes. Experience since Order

No. 1000 has also borne out the Commission’s observation that it is not in the economic self-

in an existing FERC proceeding or a proceeding in any other forum. Complainants note that the

Commission did investigate similar concerns around SPP’s prior designation of Short-Term

Reliability Projects in a Show Cause investigation in Docket No. EL19-92-000. However, that

proceeding has since terminated.

           H.    Other Processes to Resolve Complaint (18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(9) & (10))

       Neither ETCC nor IECA used FERC’s informal dispute resolution procedures. However,

ETCC members were actively involved in the SPP stakeholder process regarding SPP’s planning

and approval of Short-Term Reliability Projects under the 2025 Integrated Transmission Planning

 (“ITP”) portfolio. ETCC and individual ETCC members submitted comments to the SPP urging

SPP to not approve the Four Projects as Short-Term Reliability Projects.            SPP remained

unresponsive to the concerns raised by ETCC and several consumer and public interest

organizations. Accordingly, ETCC does not believe that any alternate dispute resolution would be

timely, effective, or a constructive use of party resources. Counsel for ETCC and IECA provided

SPP’s Executive Vice President Regulatory Policy and General Counsel with advance notice of

this Complaint the day prior to filing.

           I.    Notice of Complaint (18 C.F.R. § 385.206(b)(10))

       A form notice of Complaint is appended to the Complaint at Attachment 1.
           J.   Rule 206(b)(11): Need for Fast Track processing and why the standard
                processes are not adequate.
       The Complainants respectfully request Fast Track processing and that the Commission act

on this Complaint expeditiously. ETCC and IECA respectfully request the expeditious issuance of

an order granting the Complaint prior to the formal assignment of the underlying challenged

projects that is set to occur in early February 2027. The Commission should expedite its review

of this Complaint to prevent direct assignment of $3.8 billion in interstate, FERC-jurisdictional

transmission projects outside of a competitive solicitation process that would otherwise have

occurred under the SPP Tariff. Expeditious action on this Complaint is consistent with the

Commission’s statutory obligation to prevent consumers from paying excess rates for jurisdictional

services and to ensure that all jurisdictional rates are just and reasonable. The Commission

exercises regulatory oversight over SPP and must ensure that SPP’s practices affecting rates adhere

to SPP’s Tariff and all relevant Commission orders, including Order No. 1000.

                                       VII.    CONCLUSION

         WHEREFORE, for the reasons raised herein, Electricity Transmission Competition

 Coalition and the Industrial Energy Consumers of America request that the Commission grant

 this Complaint and find that SPP violated its Tariff and Section 206 of the Federal Power Act in

 its designation of the Four Projects in the 2025 ITP portfolio as Short-Term Reliability Projects.

                                  NOTICE OF COMPLAINT

Take notice that on October 28, 2026, the Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition and the
Industrial Energy Consumers of America (collectively, “the Complainants”) filed a formal
complaint against Southwest Power Pool, Inc. Sections 206, 306 and 309 of the Federal Power
Act, 16 U.S.C. §§ 824eand 825h and 18 C.F.R. § 385.206 (2019), requesting that the
Commission find that SPP violated Attachment Y of its Open Access Transmission Tariff by
designating four transmission projects as Short-Term Reliability Projects in the 2025 Integrated
Transmission Planning (“ITP”) portfolio. The Complaint requests a refund effective date on the
date the Complaint is filed.

         Complainants certify that copies of the Complaint were served on contacts for the public
utilities and transmission providers as listed on the Commission’s list of Corporate Officials.

        Any person desiring to intervene or to protest this filing must file in accordance with
Rules 211 and 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure (18 C.F.R. §§ 385.211
and 385.214). Protests will be considered by the Commission in determining the appropriate

        Any person wishing to become a party must file a notice of intervention or motion to
intervene, as appropriate. The Respondents’ answers and all interventions, or protests must be
filed on or before the comment date. The Respondents’ answers, motions to intervene, and
protests must be served on the Complainant.

of paper using the “eFiling link at http://www.ferc.gov. Persons unable to file electronically

19   A.   My testimony addresses:

20              A discussion of SPP governance and processes that lead to Short-Term Reliability

21               designation.

22              An explanation of SPP’s Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) requirements

23               regarding Short-Term Reliability.

 1                  An explanation as to why SPP’s 2025 ITP Assessment designations are at fault and

 2                   inconsistent with the OATT criteria in Attachment Y.

 3   Q.   PLEASE          EXPLAIN          THE   TARIFF         ATTACHMENT          Y   SECTION       I.3

 4        REQUIREMENTS THAT ARE PERTINENT TO THE COMPLAINT’S ALLEGED

 5        TARIFF VIOLATION.

 6   A.   Attachment Y Section I.3 has a variety of requirements for SPP to document and explain

 7        the       technical   analysis   corresponding   to    the   Short-Term   Reliability   Project

 8        recommendations. Critically, the Tariff requires that Short-Term Reliability projects must

 9        be “required to be in-service within 3 years or less to address an identified reliability

10        violation” in order to qualify for Short-Term Reliability Project designation. The very

11        phrase “required to be in-service within 3 years or less” mandates that the proposed

12        upgrade must be energized within the designated time window, not just preferred, or

13        desired, or wanted to be in-service and energized; required to be in-service. The Short-

14        Term Reliability Projects SPP selected in the 2025 ITP Assessment Portfolio do not meet

15        this requirement for energization and therefore are ineligible to be designated as Short-

16        Term Reliability Projects. Attachment Y Section 1.3.a requires that SPP “[s]eparately

17        identify and post an explanation of the reliability violations and system conditions for

18        which there is a time-sensitive need, in sufficient detail to allow stakeholders to understand

19        the need and why it is time sensitive.” SPP also did not sufficiently explain and justify its

20        2025 Short-Term Reliability Project determinations nor did SPP explain any non-

21        transmission alternatives, as required by Attachment Y, Section I.3 and explained in more

22        detail by Mr Konidena.

 1   II. EXPERIENCE WITH THE SPP BOARD PROCESSES
 2

15        and new approaches that have been approved and implemented into effective programs like

22        range planning. While at SPP, I was engaged in numerous Board educational sessions and

24        of strategic opportunities. Despite support from several key Board and RSC members

 5        themselves. Brattle and other assessments show that ISO/RTO data supports 20-30% lower

 6        costs from competitive bids which typically include price caps. The mere presence of a

 7        competitive bidding process provides an incentive for incumbent utilities to refine their

 8        traditional estimates, project designs and execution plans. While costs are important given

 9        the focus on affordability, the certainty of projects meeting the identified need dates is also

10        critical. Well-designed competitive bidding processes deliver timely, reliable and lower

11        cost upgrades with strong guarantees that indicate bid offered terms will protect ratepayers.

12   Q.   HAVE YOU OBSERVED INCUMBENT UTILITIES USING THEIR INFLUENCE

13        IN SPP PROCESSES?

14   A.   Yes. As explained in the affidavit testimony of Neeya Toleman (EL26-58), the incumbent

15        utilities frequently use SPP’s own processes to their benefit delaying projects or nixing

16        projects they do not want to be competitive that later become Short-Term Reliability

17        Projects because they’re still desirable projects.

18   Q.   ARE YOU AWARE OF EVIDENCE SHOWING THAT INCUMBENT UTILITIES

19        USE     THEIR       INFLUENCE          TO      MANIPULATE           THE     SHORT-TERM

20        RELIABILITY PROCESS TO THEIR BENEFIT?

21   A.   Also explained in Ms. Toleman’s testimony, the incumbent utilities consistently oppose

22        transmission expansion that is competitive but are quick to turn around and support it when

23        it is deemed Short-Term Reliability and eligible for direct assignment. In the 2025 ITP, the

 2        Draw – Minco – Seminole – Anthem 765 kV segments that were eligible for competition

 3        and voluntarily supported the transmission plan islanding 765 kV segments. Today, the

 4        same utilities advocate for connected 765 kV transmission and the need for connected

 5        paths, but in the name of near-term need dates and getting as much transmission designated

 7   Q.   DO YOU HAVE ANY OBSERVATIONS AND COMMENTS ABOUT EXISTING

 8        AND PLANNED PROCESS IMPROVEMENTS AT SPP THAT WILL AFFECT

 9        THE NEED DATE FOR TRANSMISSION UPGRADES?

10   A.   Yes. SPP has provided leadership in the industry when it comes to taking advantage of

11        new approaches and tools to improve grid operations and planning. In addition to

12        implementing economic transmission topology optimization to better manage congestion

13        costs in the near term, SPP is standing up its Intermediate Planning function to address

14        congestion and constraints associated with planned outages to maintain and upgrade

15        system capacity. The effective deployment of Advanced Transmission Technologies

16        (“ATTs”) can and should provide a bridge to the need dates of major upgrades. FERC

17        Orders 1920, 2023, and the recent Show Cause Order related to large loads require

18        transmission service providers to demonstrate that ATTs can mitigate and defer the need

19        date for large transmission expansion projects.

20        Delaying the in-service dates for select projects can lower project total costs and lessen

21        the revenue requirements imposed on consumers when line routing, ROW acquisition,

22        project design, etc. are not rushed which will in almost all cases result in a price premium

23        compared to a more prudent and cost-effective Engineering, Procurement and

 2           reasonable in-service dates for major transmission expansion projects and upgrades, ATTs

 3           provide benefits to consumers in better managing congestion and curtailments during the

 4           outages required to rebuild and upgrade many existing facilities that are critical

 5           components of the bulk power system. Intermediate Planning provides tremendous value

 6           in helping SPP achieve its mission which has been modified in the last few years to

 7           include “cost effectively” as a key attribute for SPP actions which is paramount given the

 8           focus on affordability.

 9           Particularly, the relevance to this Complaint is that Intermediate Planning has the ability

10           to identify instances where the need date far precedes the in-service date and consider

11           additional transmission mitigations in the interim as “expected to occur” needs within

12           “the three-year planning horizon”14. The process still falls short in that it can recommend

13           projects that to not meet their near-term need dates, but likely will be projects that

14           undercut the implementation timelines of large, EHV projects and help mitigate or lessen

15           the reliability issues until the larger scope, longer lead solution is in place. As such, SPP

16           has a new additional tool to mitigate near-term needs with better practicality and

17           probability of actually serving the near-term needs by preferring solutions with more

18           likely near-term in-service dates. SPP’s justification for near-term need of identified 2025

                            DIRECT TESTIMONY OF RAO KONIDENA


 1   I. INTRODUCTION
 2   Q.     PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.     My name is Rao Konidena. My business address is Roseville, Minnesota, 55113.

 4   Q.     BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 5   A.     I am employed by Rakon Energy LLC.

 6   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR POSITION AND DUTIES WITH RAKON ENERGY LLC?

 7   A.     I am the President of Rakon Energy LLC. Rakon Energy is owned and operated by me. I

 8          have provided independent consulting services for almost 9 years leveraging my wholesale

 9          energy market experience and knowledge of Regional Transmission Organization (RTO)

10          transmission planning tariff and business practices.

11   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR EDUCATIONAL AND EMPLOYMENT BACKGROUND PRIOR

12          TO RAKON ENERGY LLC?
  1   A.   I received a Bachelor of Engineering in Electrical & Electronics Engineering from

 2        Bangalore University, a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from the University

 3        of Texas at Arlington, and a Master of Business Administration from the University of

 4        Minnesota.

 5        Prior to Rakon Energy LLC, I worked in Transmission Asset Management at Midcontinent

 6        Independent System Operator (“MISO”) for almost 15 years, from September 2003 to May

 7        2018. I started as an Applications Engineer for Planning, where I ran transmission

 8        reliability studies, transmission capacity calculations, and analysis for the MISO

 9        Transmission Expansion Plan (“MTEP”).

10        I was later promoted to Lead, Resource Forecasting in 2006, responsible for a team of

11        engineers running the capacity forecasting software. That forecasting work is incorporated

12        in the MTEP non-transmission alternatives section. After a promotion to Manager of

13        Resource Forecasting in 2009, I led Demand Response and Energy Efficiency forecasting

14        for MTEP.

15        I worked in compliance, process, and project management for the Transmission Asset

16        Management (“TAM”) division as Senior Manager of TAM Operations from 2013 to 2015.

17        In this role, my team and I were responsible for division-wide financial and strategic

18        planning, supporting corporate planning and compliance efforts. I came back to the Policy

19        Studies department in the Principal Policy Advisor role for MISO in 2015, leading the

20        long-term load forecasting project with Purdue University's State Utility Forecasting Group

21        and Applied Energy Group demand response (“DR”), energy efficiency (“EE”) and

22        distributed generation (“DG”) potential study at MISO.




                                                   2
  1        Before leaving MISO in 2018, I led policy efforts on energy storage and distributed energy

 2        resources within economic transmission planning. I presented on energy storage and

 3        distributed energy resources to MISO state commissions, including the Iowa Utilities

 4        Board, the South Dakota Public Utilities Commission, and the Organization of MISO

 5        States.

 6   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

 7   A.   My testimony addresses technical investigation of SPP’s annual regional transmission

 8        planning process, the Integrated Transmission Plan, and the context for how Short-Term

 9        Reliability projects have been identified and designated.

10   Q.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY PROVIDED TESTIMONY BEFORE THE FEDERAL

11        ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION?

12   A.   Yes. I have submitted testimony and affidavits at the Federal Energy Regulatory

13        Commission (FERC) on behalf of my clients, including an affidavit for Voltus, Inc. on

14        SPP's multi-nodal aggregation (Docket No. ER22-1697); expert testimony on behalf of the

15        Kentucky Public Service Commission in a transmission cost allocation complaint (Docket

16        No. EL25-67-000); an affidavit for the Office of the People's Counsel of D.C. on PJM's

17        Reserves Pricing Proposal; an affidavit for municipal utilities in Wisconsin and Missouri

18        on MISO's Resource Adequacy construct; and an affidavit for the Missouri Joint Municipal

19        Electric Utilities Commission, Missouri River Energy Services, and WPPI Energy on

20        MISO's External Resource Zone proposal (Docket No. ER18-1173-001).




                                                   3
  1   Q.         ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 2   A.          I am testifying on behalf of Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition (ETCC).

 3   Q.         HAVE YOUR REVIEWED THE TESTIMONIES OF JAY CASPARY AND

 4              RICHARD ALLEN ON BEHALF OF THE ELECTRICITY TRANSMISSION

 5              COMPETITION COALITION IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 6   A.         Yes. I have reviewed those testimonies and worked collaboratively with Mr. Caspary and

 7              Mr. Allen regarding the development of testimonies in this proceeding.

 8   Q.         DO THE ANALYSES AND CONCLUSIONS OF MR. CASPARY AND MR. ALLEN

 9              MAKE SENSE TO YOU?

10   A.         Yes.

11   Q.         DO YOU AGREE THAT THE TESTIMONIES OF MR. CASPARY AND MR.

12              ALLEN        PROVIDE     EVIDENCE        OF    SPP    TARIFF      ATTACHMENT           Y

13              VIOLATIONS BY SPP AND THE SPP BOARD?

14   A.         Yes.


15   II. PLANNING ANALYSIS
16   Q.         HAVE YOU REVIEWED MR. CASPARY'S DESCRIPTION OF THE SHORT-

17              TERM RELIABILITY EXEMPTION IN SPP'S OPEN ACCESS TRANSMISSION

18              TARIFF ("TARIFF"), AND DO YOU AGREE WITH IT?

19   A.         Yes. I have reviewed Mr. Caspary's affidavit, which describes the Short-Term Reliability

20              exemption in Attachment Y of the Tariff.1 I agree with his explanation that Attachment Y,

21              Section I.3 establishes a narrow exception to competition for upgrades "required to be in




     1
         Caspary Affidavit at Page 13.

                                                        4
  1           service within 3 years or less to address an identified reliability violation,"2 and that the

 2           provision is permissive: SPP "may" designate the incumbent Transmission Owner under

 3           Section IV, so the Transmission Owner Selection Process (“TOSP”)/competitive bidding

 4           remains the default.3 My affidavit builds on that understanding by examining whether

 5           SPP's designation of the four 2025 ITP Short-Term Reliability Projects is supported by the

 6           record SPP provided.

 7   Q.      WHAT ARE YOUR MAIN CONCLUSIONS REGARDING THE NEED FOR THE

 8           FOUR PROJECTS IDENTIFIED IN SPP'S 2025 INTEGRATED TRANSMISSION

 9           PLANNING ("ITP") ASSESSMENT SHORT-TERM RELIABILITY PROJECTS

10           REPORT?

11   A.      In the 2025 Integrated Transmission Planning (“ITP”) Assessment, SPP has designated the

12           following four projects as short-term reliability projects4, per Attachment Y of its Tariff.

13               1. Crawfish Draw – Phantom 765 kV New Line

14               2. Crosstown – Blue Valley Station 161 kV New Line

15               3. North Hays – Chetolah Creek 115 kV New Line

16               4. Seminole – Southwest Shreveport 765 kV New Line

17           While I conclude that there is a reliability need for the four projects, I do not conclude that

18           SPP is justified in designating these four projects as short-term reliability projects and

19           subsequently waiving the TOSP.

20   Q.      IN YOUR OPINION, HAS SPP MITIGATED SHORT-TERM RELIABILITY



     2
       Tariff, Attachment Y, Section I.3.
     3
       Caspary Affidavit at Page 15.
     4
       2025 INTEGRATED TRANSMISSION PLANNING ASSESSMENT, SHORT-TERM RELIABILITY
     PROJECTS REPORT, By SPP ENGINEERING, Published on 12/09/2025, Version 1.0
     https://www.spp.org/documents/75446/2025%20itp%20short-term%20reliability%20projects%20report.pdf.
     (“STRP Report”).

                                                         5
  1            NEEDS TO THE LEVEL THE TARIFF REQUIRES?

 2   A.       No. SPP's Attachment Y, Section I.3. of the Tariff which SPP references in the 2025 Short-

 3            Term Reliability Project report to lay the foundation for the four Short-Term Reliability

 4            Projects requires SPP to designate a Short-Term Reliability Project "if such upgrade is

 5            required to be in service within 3 years or less to address an identified reliability violation"5.

 6                     SPP identified solutions to address Need dates within the 3 years and yet its own

 7            Staging6 criteria (60-month lead time for both Crawfish Draw – Phantom and Seminole –

 8            Southwest Shreveport) admits that building a 765 kV solution is infeasible within 3 years.

 9            In other words, the Short-Term Reliability Project designation is only for upgrades that are

10            “required to be in service within 3 years or less to address an identified reliability violation”

11            – that's the explicit Tariff language. SPP picked 765 kV solutions for the reliability

12            violations – that part meets the intent of the Tariff, but, SPP does not meet the intent of the

13            "required to be in service within 3 years or less" part of the Tariff because building 765 kV

14            solutions within 3 years or less is infeasible and extremely challenging for EHV (ex. 345

15            kV and above) for Short-Term Reliability exemption qualification. The very identification

16            of Crawfish Draw – Phantom and its designation as a Short-Term Reliability Project is a

17            byproduct of this siloed way of interpreting and implementing the Tariff. The natural

18            follow up question that is relevant then is, how does SPP plan to address the identified

19            reliability violation if the 765 kV solution is not built within the required 3 years or less?

20                     One possible answer is that SPP is aware of the history of these operational issues




     5
       Attachment Y, Section I.3."For any upgrade meeting the specifications listed in Section I.1 of this Attachment Y,
     the Transmission Provider may designate the Transmission Owner(s) in accordance with Section IV of this
     Attachment Y if such upgrade is required to be in service within 3 years or less to address an identified reliability
     violation (“Short-Term Reliability Project”). "
     6
       Section 6.7. Staging, 277-page 2025 ITP Assessments Report.

                                                               6
  1        that drove the reliability violations because the operational issues did not show up suddenly

 2        in the 2025 analysis as the commentary below indicates. Furthermore, SPP does not expect

 3        the upgrades to be in place within the required 3-year-or-less requirement, which would

 4        indicate these upgrades are not Short-Term Reliability Projects. As part of SPP’s process,

 5        all reliability projects that do not meet their stated needs require mitigation plans to ensure

 6        reliability until the project’s energization. In the case of many Short-Term Reliability

 7        Projects driven by large load interconnection, the mitigation has been stated as load

 8        interconnection deferment. The issue before FERC today is SPP’s blatant disregard for

 9        project lead times, which by design do not actually mitigate needs as the Tariff requires.

10               SPP is compounding the error of not following its Tariff - the "required to be in

11        service within 3 years or less" part of the Tariff, with the Short-Term Reliability Project

12        designations that picks winners (incumbent Transmission Owners) and losers (competitive

13        transmission developers). Specifically, in the Southwest Public Service Company’s

14        (“SPS”) area, SPP repeatedly choosing long-lead 765 kV projects to mitigate short-term

15        reliability needs sets up a perpetual waterfall of 765 kV Short-Term Reliability Projects

16        until the first project comes online, a methodology that is neither robust nor truly serving

17        customers.

18   Q.   HAS SPP PROVIDED THE TARIFF REQUIRED JUSTIFICATION FOR THE

19        SHORT-TERM RELIABILITY NEED?

20   A.   No. SPP's Attachment Y, Transmission Owner Designation Process, Section I.3.a states

21        that, SPP shall "[s]eparately identify and post an explanation of the reliability violations

22        and system conditions for which there is a time-sensitive need, in sufficient detail to allow

23        stakeholders to understand the need and why it is time sensitive."



                                                    7
  1                  SPP's Attachment Y Section I.3.b.i also states that SPP will provide "an explanation

 2          of other transmission or non-transmission options that the Transmission Provider

 3          considered but concluded would not sufficiently address the immediate reliability need."

 4                  As I will describe below, SPP provided neither the "sufficient detail" to justify the

 5          "time-sensitive need" nor an explanation of other "non-transmission options" that SPP

 6          considered but concluded would not sufficiently address the immediate reliability need for

 7          the four Short-Term Reliability projects.

 8   Q.     WERE YOU ABLE TO INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATE THE NEED DATE

 9          ANALYSIS?

10   A.     No. As I describe below in sufficient detail, I was unable to independently corroborate the

11          need date analysis. In fact, my analysis based on SPP's Needs Assessment spreadsheets

12          from past ITPs indicates that there is a need for the four projects but not as short-term

13          reliability need.

14   Q.     WHY IS SPP'S YEAR-FIVE AND YEAR-TEN ANALYSIS RELEVANT TO

15          PROJECTS THAT MUST BE NEEDED WITHIN THREE YEARS?

16   A.     SPP’s long term five- and ten-year analysis is relevant because those data points are also

17          used in SPP's staging process that determines each project's need date, and the need date

18          determines whether a project falls within the three-year window for a Short-Term

19          Reliability Project. In the 2025 ITP, SPP studied three model years: year two (2026), year

20          five (2029), and year ten (2034).7 The ITP Manual stages each reliability project "based on

21          the year and season when the needs addressed by each project appear on the transmission

     https://www.spp.org/documents/73387/2025%20itp%20assessment%20scope_v4.0.pdf.

                                                        8
  1            system."8 Upgrades that solve year-two violations are staged to the corresponding season

 2            of year two. For needs that first appear in year five or year ten, the Manual requires a linear

 3            interpolation between the model in which the violation appears and the previous model on

 4            record.9 As a result, a need that first appears in the 2029 model can receive an interpolated

 5            need date in 2027 or 2028, within three years. SPP described this process to FERC,

 6            explaining that it determines need dates under the staging criteria in Section 6.3 of the ITP

 7            Manual and that a project may be deemed a Short-Term Reliability Project if the need date

 8            resulting from that process falls within three years.10 My review of SPP's year-two, year-

 9            five and year-ten results is therefore how I tested whether SPP's need dates, and the Short-

10            Term Reliability Projects designations that depend on them, follow SPP's own process.

11   Q.       WERE YOU ABLE TO INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATE THE NEED DATE

10   Q.   WHAT GAPS IN SPP’S PLANNING PROCESS DID YOU OBSERVE IN YOUR

11        INVESTIGATION?

12   A.   One of the gaps in SPP’s planning process that my analysis highlights is the lack of

13        traceability from reliability violations to the Short-Term Reliability Projects. Another gap

14        is that is not clear to me how SPP arrived at the Short-Term Reliability Project designations

15        when a) extrapolation or incorrect application of interpolation of needs occurred to

16        determine the need date, b) ratings were changing, c) load was not forecasted in 10-year

17        out models, d) monitoring definitions were changing, e) the impact of load shed events on

18        rating changes was uncertain, and f) the level of consideration given to non-transmission

19        or alternative solutions that are not as long-lead was unclear. All these gaps cumulatively

20        make the Short-Term Reliability Project need determination an uncorroborated

21        designation.

22   Q.   HOW HAVE THOSE GAPS CREATED THE SHORT-TERM RELIABILITY

23        ISSUES OF TODAY?


                                                   82
  1   A.         The gaps work together in two ways. Most of them cause needs to appear suddenly, or

 2              earlier than they otherwise would, in a later ITP cycle, which shortens the time available

 3              to address them so that they fall within the three-year window for a Short-Term Reliability

 4              Project. The remaining gaps prevent stakeholders from testing whether those needs and

 5              their timing are real.

 6              1. Changing inputs cause needs to appear abruptly in a later cycle. When load forecasts,

 7                  flowgate ratings and monitoring definitions change between ITP cycles, a need that

 8                  was absent or distant in one cycle can appear in the near-term models of the next. As

 9                  discussed above, [BEGIN CEII] the 10-year load forecasts showed little growth in the

10                  2020 through 2023 ITPs and then increased starting in the 2024 ITP; the SPSNMTIES

11                  flowgate was redefined in 2023, changing the facilities it monitors; and the

12                  SPPSPSTIES and PSOSWEPCOTIE ratings changed without changes in the

13                  underlying branch data. [END CEII] Each of these can move a need from the later

14                  years of the planning horizon into the near term. Once a need appears in the near-term

15                  models, the time left to address it through the standard process is short, and the project

16                  becomes a candidate for Short-Term Reliability designation.

17              2. The need-date method can move the need date earlier. The ITP Manual stages

18                  reliability needs by the year and season in which they appear, using interpolation for

19                  needs first appearing in year five or year ten.160 As discussed above, the need dates for

20                  Crawfish Draw – Phantom and Seminole – Southwest Shreveport cannot be derived

21                  from those staging criteria. A need date set earlier than the staging criteria support

22                  places the project inside the three-year window, and SPP told FERC that a project may

 3           3. Limited consideration of alternatives leaves only long-lead solutions. Without a

 4               documented evaluation of shorter-lead options, such as FACTS devices or other non-

 5               transmission options/solutions, SPP selected 765 kV projects whose projected in-

 6               service dates fall years after their need dates. The underlying needs therefore remain

 7               unresolved in the interim and can continue to appear in each new ITP’s near-term

 8               models, producing further short-term needs until the long-lead projects are in service.

 9           4. The lack of traceability prevents stakeholders from testing any of this. Because SPP’s

10               Short-Term Reliability Project Report does not trace each Short-Term Reliability

11               Project to specific reliability violations, model inputs, and rating or definition changes,

12               and because the effect of the load shed events on the rating changes is not documented,

13               stakeholders cannot determine whether a given Short-Term Reliability need reflects

14               actual system conditions or changes in the planning inputs. That is the information the

15               Tariff requires SPP to provide, “in sufficient detail to allow stakeholders to understand

16               the need and why it is time sensitive.”162

                              UNITED STATES OF AMERICA

                           DIRECT TESTIMONY OF RICHARD ALLEN


 1   I. INTRODUCTION

 2   Q.     PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

 3   A.     My name is Richard Allen. My business address is Malta, New York 12020.

 4   Q.     BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED?

 5   A.     Clean Grid Consulting, LLC.

 6   Q.     WHAT IS YOUR CURRENT POSITION WITH CLEAN GRID CONSULTING,

 7          LLC?

 8   A.     I am the President and sole member of Clean Grid Consulting, LLC.

 9   Q.     WHAT ARE YOUR DUTIES IN YOUR CURRENT POSITION?

10   A.     I advise transmission developers, utilities, and financial institutions on electric

11          transmission development, regulatory strategy, and transmission operations. My work

12          includes supporting competitive transmission proposal development through strategic

13          guidance, competitive analysis, cost containment strategies, and proposal preparation

                                                   1
                                                                             Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                           Complainant Exhibit C

 1        support. I advise on transmission project development for competitive and directly

 2        assigned projects, including execution strategies, construction approaches, project

 3        management, procurement, and permitting. I advise investment firms evaluating

 4        transmission asset opportunities, including assessment of regulatory, commercial, and

 5        project risks. I also consult on transmission operating models and provide guidance on

 6        Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) formula rate matters and related cost

 7        recovery.

 8   Q.   HOW LONG HAVE YOU BEEN EMPLOYED BY CLEAN GRID CONSULTING

 9        LLC?

10   A.   I formed Clean Grid Consulting, LLC in 2023 and have been actively consulting since then.

11   Q.   WHAT WAS YOUR EDUCATIONAL AND EMPLOYMENT BACKGROUND

12        PRIOR TO JOINING CLEAN GRID CONSULTING?

13   A.   I graduated from Clarkson University in 1987 with a Bachelor of Science in Electrical

14        Engineering. In 1989, I received a Master of Electric Power Engineering degree from

15        Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. In 2004, I received a Master of Business Administration

16        from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute.

17        I joined Commonwealth Electric in 1987 as a Junior Engineer in the Engineering

18        Department responsible for transmission and substation design. In 1989, I joined Central

19        Hudson as a Distribution Planning engineer. In 1991, I joined Niagara Mohawk

20        Corporation (now National Grid) as a substation design engineer and project manager

21        where I designed new high voltage substations and capital improvements to existing

22        substations, managing the permitting, construction, and commissioning of substation

23        projects in a challenging regulatory environment. In 1995, I was promoted to the position


                                                   2
                                                                         Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                       Complainant Exhibit C

 1   of Power Delivery Supervisor responsible for the construction, operation, and maintenance

 2   of high voltage electric substations. In 1999, I assumed the position of Relay Supervisor

 3   responsible for the installation, operation, and maintenance of the electric system

 4   protection and controls as well as testing and commissioning of major electric power

 5   equipment and facilities. In 2003, I was transferred to the position of Senior Engineer in

 6   Transmission Planning, performing load flow analysis and congestion analysis. In March

 7   2005, I was promoted to the position of Lead Project Manager where I managed major

 8   infrastructure improvement projects including power plant interconnections, new and

 9   upgraded transmission lines, and substation expansions. In December 2009, I was

10   promoted to Director of Business Development where I was responsible for identifying,

11   analyzing, and implementing business growth opportunities across the United States. In

12   this role I was a principal contributor to the establishment of the New York Transco and

13   served as its first Vice President of Capital Investments.

14   In 2015, I joined the New York Power Authority (“NYPA”) as the Vice President of Project

15   and Business Development. In this role I was responsible for identifying, developing and

16   permitting new transmission, renewable, and energy storage projects.

17   In 2019, I joined NextEra Energy Transmission (“NEET”) to become the President of

18   NEET’s New York (“NEETNY”) electric transmission operating company. In this role, I

19   was responsible for NEETNY’s financial performance, regulatory relations, operations,

20   and transmission development. I was responsible for the construction of the first

21   competitively awarded project in New York, the Empire State Line. In 2020 and 2022, I

22   assumed the roles of President of NEET’s New England and Canadian transmission




                                               3
                                                                             Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                           Complainant Exhibit C

 1        operating companies, respectively, with responsibilities similar to those I had with

 2        NEETNY. I retired from NEET in 2023 and began my current role.

 3   Q.   HAVE YOU PREVIOUSLY PROVIDED TESTIMONY BEFORE THE FEDERAL

 4        ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION?

 5   A.   Yes, I provided testimony in FERC Docket No. EL26-58-000 and in FERC Docket ER15-

 6        572-000.

 7   Q.   ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

 8   A.   The Electricity Transmission Competition Coalition.

 9   Q.   HAVE YOU REVIEWED THE TESTIMONIES OF RAO KONIDENA AND JAY

10        CASPARY SUBMITTED ON BEHALF OF THE ELECTRICITY TRANSMISSION

11        COMPETITION COALITION IN THIS PROCEEDING?

12   A.   Yes. I have reviewed those testimonies as they relate to the project development issues

13        addressed in my testimony and have considered how their analyses relate to my own.

14   Q.   HOW DOES THEIR TESTIMONY RELATE TO SUBJECTS ADDRESSED IN

15        YOUR TESTIMONY?

16   A.   Mr. Konidena addresses SPP’s identification and timing of the reliability needs underlying

17        the four projects designated as Short-Term Reliability Projects in the 2025 ITP. Mr.

18        Caspary addresses SPP’s decision-making process, its application of the Short-Term

19        Reliability Project designation, and the protections available through competitive

20        transmission solicitations. My testimony addresses the development activities and expected

21        timeframes for major transmission projects and whether the physical development

22        requirements support excluding those projects from competition based on schedule. The




                                                  4
                                                                                Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                              Complainant Exhibit C

 1        three testimonies address different but related aspects of the issues presented in the

 2        complaint.

 3   Q.   WHAT ISSUES DOES YOUR TESTIMONY ADDRESS, AND HOW DO THOSE

 4        ISSUES RELATE TO THE UNDERLYING COMPLAINT?

 5   A.   My testimony addresses the development cycle and expected timeframes for major

 6        transmission projects generally, with particular emphasis on extra-high-voltage projects. I

 7        discuss the development activities required under both direct assignment and competitive

 8        development and whether conducting a competitive solicitation would necessarily result in

 9        a later in-service date than could reasonably be achieved through direct assignment. I also

10        address the practical feasibility of developing, constructing, and placing major

11        transmission projects in service within three years. Finally, I apply these considerations to

12        SPP’s designation of certain projects as Short-Term Reliability Projects, including the

13        Crawfish Draw–Phantom and Seminole–Southwest Shreveport 765 kV projects.

14   II. EXPERIENCE WITH TRANSMISSION DEVELOPMENT
15
16   Q.   WHAT IS YOUR EXPERIENCE DEVELOPING DIRECTLY ASSIGNED OR

17        NON-COMPETITIVE TRANSMISSION PROJECTS?

18   A.   My experience is broad and extensive. I have experience across the full project

19        development cycle—from origination to commercial operation. In my roles with National

20        Grid (Niagara Mohawk) as a Transmission Planner, I performed load flow and

21        production cost analysis to identify any transmission improvements necessary to improve

22        system reliability and economic performance. As a design engineer, I designed new and

23        expanded substations. As a Project Manager, I managed transmission line projects, up to

24        345 kV, from conception through permitting, engineering, construction, and operations.


                                                   5
                                                                              Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                            Complainant Exhibit C

 1        As Director of Business Development, I performed due diligence on potential

 2        transmission acquisitions and originated transmission projects. In my role with NYPA, I

 3        led the teams responsible for originating transmission line projects and advanced the

 4        permitting of the Smart Path transmission project. In my role with NEET, I led the team

 5        responsible for the origination and expansion of a transmission project for New

 6        Hampshire Transmission and origination of transmission line projects for NEETNY.

 7   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF YOUR EXPERIENCE WITH

 8        COMPETITIVE TRANSMISSION SOLICITATIONS IN THE SPP REGION.

 9   A.   I have advised incumbent transmission owners and independent transmission developers

10        in preparing proposals for three SPP competitive solicitations: Lynch – Medanos 115 kV,

11        Mathewson – Redbud 345 kV, and Wolf Creek – Blackberry 345 kV.

12   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE AN OVERVIEW OF YOUR EXPERIENCE WITH

13        COMPETITIVE TRANSMISSION SOLICITATIONS IN ANY OTHER REGIONS.

14   A.   My initial experience with competitive transmission solicitations was in New York, where

15        I led the investor-owned utilities’ response to a New York Public Service Commission

16        proceeding that comparatively evaluated transmission solutions for a congested

17        transmission corridor (Case No. 12-T-0502). I later led or supported proposal teams for

18        the NYISO Western New York, AC Transmission, and Long Island Offshore Wind

19        solicitations. Following the selection of the NYPA and LS Power proposal in the AC

20        Transmission solicitation, I continued to lead NYPA’s participation during the initial

21        development until I left NYPA in 2019. I supported a response to ISO New England’s

22        Greater Boston solicitation and provided advisory support for four MISO competitive

23        solicitations. I also had executive responsibility for developing and constructing the


                                                  6
                                                                              Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                            Complainant Exhibit C

 1        competitively awarded Empire State Line in New York.

 2   Q.   BEFORE YOUR CURRENT EMPLOYMENT, DID YOU SUCCESSFULLY WIN

 3        ANY COMPETITIVE TRANSMISSION SOLICITATIONS?

 4   A.   Yes, during my employment with NYPA, I negotiated a joint development agreement

 5        with LS Power to jointly participate in the NYISO AC Transmission Public Policy

 6        solicitation and led the NYPA team in preparing the response. The NYPA and LS Power

 7        proposal was selected by NYISO.

 8        Additionally, during my tenure at National Grid, I led the development of a joint proposal

 9        submitted on behalf of the New York investor-owned utilities in the NYPSC’s first state-

10        driven competitive transmission process. NYPSC Staff ranked the joint utilities’ proposal

11        as the highest rated submission, but the NYPSC ultimately referred the identified need to

12        NYISO before making an award.

13   Q.   HAVE YOU OBSERVED ANY DIFFERENCES BETWEEN THE

14        DEVELOPMENT AND EXECUTION OF DIRECTLY ASSIGNED OR NON-

15        COMPETITIVE AND COMPETITIVELY AWARDED PROJECTS?

16   A.   Yes. Competitive projects are developed against the commitments contained in the

17        selected proposal and the resulting project agreement or notification to construct. Those

18        commitments commonly include a defined project scope, cost containment terms,

19        schedule commitment, reporting requirements, and financial consequences for failing to

20        meet certain commitments. Those obligations create discipline and accountability from

21        the beginning of development. Directly assigned or non-competitive projects generally

22        proceed under the incumbent owner's ordinary internal development and cost recovery

23        processes. Although those processes may be effective, the direct assignment itself does


                                                   7
                                                                             Docket No. EL27-___
                                                                           Complainant Exhibit C

 1        not ordinarily create the same competitive pressure to challenge design assumptions,

 2        delivery methods, costs, or schedules, and it often does not provide comparable binding

 3        cost and schedule protections for customers.

 4   Q.   PLEASE PROVIDE A GENERAL DESCRIPTION OF THE DEVELOPMENT OF

 5        A TRANSMISSION PROJECT, INCLUDING ANY DIFFERENCES BETWEEN A

 6        DIRECTLY ASSIGNED AND A COMPETITIVELY AWARDED PROJECT IN

 7        SPP.

 8   A.   In SPP, the development sequence is substantially the same whether a project is directly

 9        assigned or competitively awarded. Regardless of how the developer is selected,

10        development of the project requires routing and preliminary engineering, siting and

11        environmental approvals, acquisition of land and easements, detailed engineering,

12        procurement of long-lead equipment and construction services, construction, testing, and

 3   Q.   PLEASE EXPLAIN A NORMAL OR EXPECTED TIME BY WHICH A 345 kV

 4        TRANSMISSION PROJECT COULD BE COMPLETED.

 5   A.   It is difficult to define a single normal development period for a 345 kV transmission line

 6        because the schedule depends heavily on the scope and location of the project. Relevant

 7        factors include the length and terrain of the route, whether the project requires a new right-

 8        of-way or can use an existing corridor, the number of affected landowners and jurisdictions,

 9        the extent of the associated substation and terminal work, state and federal permitting

10        requirements including environmental reviews, equipment and material lead times,

11        workforce availability, outage requirements, and seasonal construction constraints.

12        In my experience, approximately four to seven years from project approval to in-service

13        operation is a reasonable planning range for a greenfield 345 kV project. A shorter or less

14        complex project may be completed in less time, while a longer project, a project requiring

15        extensive federal or state approvals, or a project facing significant routing, land-

16        acquisition, environmental, or public opposition issues may require more time.

17        Preliminary engineering, routing, and preparation of permit applications may require

18        approximately 12 to 18 months. The permitting review process may require approximately

19        12 to 30 months or more. Land acquisition, detailed engineering, procurement, and early

20        construction planning commonly proceed concurrently with those activities when

21        circumstances    permit.   Construction,    testing,   and   commissioning     may require

22        approximately 18 to 36 months or more. These periods should not be added together

23        because substantial portions of the work ordinarily overlap.

14        or litigation, equipment lead times, and construction conditions. Regional characteristics

17        encounter fewer conflicts with existing development but may require longer routes, affect

21        transmission projects across regions, but they should not be understood as fixed schedules

22        applicable to every project. Each project must be evaluated based on its particular scope,

23        location, permitting requirements, and execution risks.
